note: Reaches 100 percent jailbreak success across the major frontier models using simple adaptive search.
title: Jailbreaking Leading Safety-Aligned LLMs with Simple Adaptive Attacks

reading.body:
Simple adaptive attacks achieve 100 percent jailbreak success against every major frontier model tested, including systems specifically hardened against prior attack methods.

The researchers used random search optimization to craft adversarial suffixes appended to user requests. For models that expose log probabilities, they designed templates targeting high probability of unsafe tokens. For models without such access, they deployed transfer attacks and prefilling exploits. The method worked uniformly across GPT-4o, Llama-3, Gemma, Claude variants, and over a dozen other frontier models. Notably, even R2D2, which was adversarially trained specifically to resist earlier jailbreak techniques, fell to this approach.

This reveals a fundamental fragility in deployed safety systems. Each model's unique architecture and API characteristics enabled targeted adaptation, suggesting that safety properties are not robust but rather brittle surfaces that adapt to specific attack patterns. Organizations relying on these systems for sensitive applications cannot treat published safety benchmarks as reliable assurances of actual behavior.

The reproducibility of these attacks means the techniques are trivially available to any actor with API access and basic optimization knowledge. This does not indicate the scale at which jailbreaks become operationally significant, the prevalence of actual misuse, or how easily new training methods might close these specific attack vectors. But it does show that current defenses are substantially weaker than the safety marketing around these models suggests.

explain_beginner: AI chat companies build in safety training specifically so their models will refuse harmful requests, and this paper tests how strong that refusal training actually is against a determined but not especially sophisticated attacker. Andriushchenko and coauthors built simple, adaptive attack methods, including one that automatically searches for a short suffix of text to add to a harmful request, tuned to nudge the model toward starting its answer with a word like "Sure" instead of refusing, and other methods based on transferring an attack that works on one model to a different one, or exploiting how a model's conversation continues after a partial, pre-filled response. Testing this approach against essentially every major safety focused chat model available at the time, including systems from OpenAI, Google, Meta, and Anthropic, and even a model that had been specifically trained to resist an earlier well known attack method, they achieved a 100 percent success rate getting the models to comply with harmful requests, as judged by another AI system. The paper's clear message is that current safety training, across the entire industry at the time of testing, does not hold up against attacks specifically adapted to how each individual model and its access method actually works.
explain_business: This paper is a direct warning to any organization relying on a foundation model provider's built in safety training as its primary or only defense against generating harmful content, since the authors achieved 100 percent jailbreak success against essentially the full roster of major safety aligned commercial and open models available at the time of testing, including one, R2D2, that had been specifically hardened against an earlier well known attack and still failed against an adapted one. The practical consequence for procurement and risk teams is that a vendor's published safety benchmark performance, at the time this paper was released, was not a reliable predictor of resistance to a motivated, adaptive attacker, since these attacks are reproducible with modest engineering effort and the authors released their code. Organizations deploying LLMs in any customer facing or unsupervised setting should not treat vendor safety alignment alone as sufficient, and should add independent output filtering, monitoring, and use case specific guardrails on top of whatever safety training the underlying model provider has already applied.
explain_practitioner: The authors combine three adaptive attack techniques, for models exposing token log probabilities, a random search procedure iteratively optimizes an adversarial suffix appended to a hand crafted jailbreak template, maximizing the log probability of the target model beginning its response with an affirmative token like Sure, for models without exposed log probabilities they use transfer attacks carrying successful suffixes across model families, and for certain APIs they exploit response prefilling, directly seeding the start of the model's reply. Evaluated with GPT-4 as an automated judge, the combined approach reaches a 100 percent attack success rate across a wide range of models including Vicuna-13B, Mistral-7B, Phi-3-Mini, Nemotron-4-340B, multiple Llama-2 and Llama-3 Chat variants, Gemma-7B, GPT-3.5, GPT-4o, and Claude models, notably including R2D2, a model from the HarmBench suite specifically adversarially trained to resist the earlier GCG attack method, which the authors found remained vulnerable in part because it proved unusually sensitive to in-context learning style prompts. The authors state plainly that adaptivity, tailoring the attack to each target model's specific architecture and API surface, was essential to the result, a generic one size fits all attack did not achieve comparable success, which is itself an implicit limitation, the attacks require per model tuning rather than working unmodified out of the box.
